title: What is a String in Java: a sequence of characters, immutable (cannot be changed after creation).
shortTitle: What is a String in Java
keyPoints: A String in Java is an immutable object that wraps a sequence of characters and cannot be modified after creation.
Every operation like concat, substring, or toUpperCase returns a new String and leaves the original unchanged.
String literals are interned in the String pool so identical literals share a single object in memory.
Always compare String contents with equals, never with the double-equals operator which checks object identity.
Use StringBuilder for efficient string building in loops because repeated concatenation creates many throwaway objects.
The String class is declared final so it cannot be subclassed, which protects the immutability guarantee.

s1_definition.oneliner: A String is an immutable sequence of characters in Java: you never change it, you only create a new one.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **String** – an object of the `java.lang.String` class that holds a sequence of characters and cannot be modified after creation.
- **Immutable** – once a String is created, its internal character data never changes; every modification method returns a new String.
- **String pool** – a special memory area where the JVM stores interned String literals so identical literals share one object.
- **final class** – `String` is declared `final`, so no subclass can override its behaviour and break the immutability contract.
- **equals vs ==** – use `equals()` to compare character content; `==` compares object references and can give wrong results for Strings created with `new`.
s1_definition.analogy: A String is like a printed cheque at National Bank of India. Once the cheque is printed with Rajesh Kumar and an amount, you cannot erase and rewrite it. If you need a different amount, you print a new cheque. The old cheque still exists exactly as printed. That is why a String never changes: any modification produces a new String, like printing a fresh cheque.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A String in Java is an object representing a sequence of characters, and its single most important property is immutability. Once a String is created, its contents can never change. Every method that appears to modify a String, such as `substring`, `concat`, or `toUpperCase`, actually returns a brand new String and leaves the original completely untouched. The String class is declared `final`, so it cannot be subclassed, and its backing data is `private final`, which locks down the immutability guarantee.

In the banking project at National Bank of India, this property is what makes PII masking safe. When Rajesh masks an account ID to show only the first two characters, the masking produces a new String, and the real account ID stored in memory and the database is never altered, which is critical for auditing. The same property allows Strings to be shared freely across threads without synchronisation and used as HashMap keys, because an immutable object has a hash code that never changes after creation.

The practical consequence every developer must remember is comparison. Because a String literal written in code is interned in the String pool while a String created with the `new` keyword is a separate object, two Strings can hold the same characters but be different objects in memory. Always compare String contents with the `equals` method, never with the double-equals operator, because double-equals compares object identity and would silently fail when a value read from a database or a web form does not happen to be the same pooled object as a literal in your code.

For performance, use StringBuilder when building a String in a loop, because repeated concatenation of immutable Strings creates many throwaway objects and makes the loop O(n squared). Pre-size the StringBuilder when the approximate output size is known to avoid repeated buffer resizing.

Remember one sentence: a String in Java is immutable, so every modification creates a new object, and you must use `equals` for content comparison and `StringBuilder` for efficient building.
